title: Asymmetric exchange and robin scheduler notes
body:
Context:
This note collects experiment observations and a loose design for an asymmetric exchange primitive + "robin" scheduling strategy to improve multi-GPU serving tail latency and utilization in heterogeneous clusters. Focus: inference serving (KV cache-heavy workloads, variable sequence lengths), interplay with NCCL tuning, and graceful fallback when full collectives are suboptimal.

Summary of idea:
- Asymmetric exchange: allow different peers to send/receive uneven tensor amounts during a collective phase. Useful when shards hold imbalanced KV cache populations or have different compute capabilities (A100 vs H100, PCIe vs NVLink zones).
- Robin scheduler: round-robin style microbatch assignment with adaptive preference scoring so that hot-keys / long sequences are steered to capable shards while keeping pairwise exchange patterns predictable for NCCL/HPC topologies.

Why we need this:
- Current symmetric sharding + allreduce/NCCL patterns assume equal-sized tensors and uniform peers. For real traffic we see 10-30% variation in KV sizes and heavy tail sequences that blow up latency for the unlucky request mapped to a slow shard.
- Conservative ring collectives can cause global slowdowns; redoing the collective to exclude slow peers is expensive. Need opportunistic asymmetric paths and fast NCCL fallback choices.

Design components:
1) KV tiling and placement metadata:
- Maintain lightweight per-shard stats: recent-quantiles for KV entry counts, median response time, PCIe hop count. Updated every 1000 requests.
- Use tiling policy that allows fractional KV ownership (e.g., shard A owns 0.6 of a hot prefix range, shard B 0.4). This reduces tail by not forcing exact balance.

2) Robin scheduler (microbatch assignment):
- Microbatch window = 16ms by default. Scheduler builds microbatches and assigns them to shards in round-robin, but weights are adjusted by a score: score = capacity_score * (1 - recent_tail_penalty) * affinity_bonus
- affinity_bonus derived from cached prefixes: if shard holds >X% prefix hits for a request, give +score.
- If a shard reports high KV-population (> threshold), steer new long-seq requests away and instead route short/embedding calls.

3) Asymmetric exchange protocol:
- Exchange phase supports vector of (peer_id, bytes_to_send). Orchestration collects a lightweight plan before kernel launch: plan exchanges with sizes.
- Kernel selection: prefer hierarchical NCCL (tree collectives) for imbalanced exchanges when network fabric indicates cross-host NVLink less likely. Use NCCL ring for near-equal sizes.
- Provide a fast path: if peer sizes are below micro-threshold (8KB), pack them and issue a single all-to-all-v with p2p buffer.

4) NCCL tuning heuristics:
- Probe stage at pod startup: run microbenchmarks to determine preferred collective (ring vs tree) for different message sizes and peer subsets. Persist heuristics in node-local cache.
- Auto-disable fused ring for imbalanced loads: if disparity ratio > 3x, switch to hierarchical tree with partial replication for hot keys.
- Use NCCL P2P for within-host, fallback to PCIe-accelerated memcpy for cross-host small exchanges to reduce kernel launch overhead.

5) Fallback / degradation modes:
- If a peer fails to respond in X ms, transiently mark it as slow and replan the exchange excluding it; use replication (send a read-only copy) for subsequent requests until rebalancing completes.
- Graceful degradation: allow slightly stale KV read (staleness threshold configurable) for better tail guarantees on user-facing endpoints.

Experiments and measured numbers (representative):
- Baseline symmetric ring, 8xA100 (NVLink host-local): p50=18ms, p95=112ms p99=240ms, throughput=850 req/s
- Robin + asymmetric-exchange, same HW: p50=16ms, p95=72ms p99=140ms, throughput=910 req/s (+7%)
- Heterogeneous 4xA100 + 4xH100 with faulty network hop: baseline p99=480ms, with asymmetric+robin p99=190ms (dramatic), throughput +15%
- Microbenchmark: tree collective favored when median message > 64KB and disparity ratio > 2.5x.

Open implementation challenges:
- Memory accounting when fractional ownership: how to enforce eviction without cross-shard coordination cost? Proposal: soft ownership with lease tokens; eviction triggers local demotion and async rebalancer.
- Complexity of pre-planning exchanges every microbatch: CPU overhead vs benefit. Need a lightweight plan data structure (fixed-size lanes) and C++ fast path.
- Interop with quantized kernels: packing/tiling must preserve alignment for 4-bit/8-bit kernels.
- Observability: trace plan decisions and NCCL mode selected per-request. Add per-request tags to tracing headers for offline eval.

Short-term action items (owner -> Asha):
- Build a synthetic bench that injects KV-skewed traffic (zipfian with hot prefixes) and measures p95/p99 across different fabric configs. (JIRA: JIRA-SS-102).
- Add node-local NCCL probe and expose heuristics via /metrics endpoint. (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842).
- Prototype a lightweight plan allocator in C++: fixed 8-lane plan, zero-copy pointers. Aim for <200ns planning overhead. (Assigned: Miguel).
- Short doc for SRE on safe rollback toggles for asymmetric-exchange on Dedicated clusters. (Confluence link above).

Longer-term ideas:
- Combine with model-slicing: if a shard is overloaded, push execution for later layers to a different shard (pipeline-like), keeping KV lookups local. This requires consistent KV snapshotting or fast replication.
- Consider an online learning layer that tunes weight multipliers for Robin scheduler per-customer workload.

Unresolved questions for architecture sync:
- What is acceptable KV staleness for enterprise customers? Need product alignment.
- Can we guarantee memory isolation with fractional ownership, or will we need hard caps per-shard?
- How often should probes run in production to capture dynamic fabric changes without creating noise?

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a sketch; the goal is to surface tradeoffs and feasibility. Please comment with concrete microbench workloads you want measured and any historical incidents where symmetric collectives caused outages (link them).

Appendix: quick pseudo-plan format
- header: batch_id, epoch, plan_ts
- lanes: [(peer0, bytes0), (peer1, bytes1), ...] up to 8 lanes
- fallback_bitmap: bitmask marking peers excluded if timeout
- kernel_hint: {"ring"|"tree"|"p2p"}

End.
